_meta.indication: SOLOSEC is a nitroimidazole antimicrobial indicated for the treatment of bacterial vaginosis in adult women.

pivotal_trials.design: Multi-center, prospective, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study; patients randomized 2:1 to a single 2 gram oral dose of SYM-1219 versus placebo, self-administered on Day 1.
pivotal_trials.population: Non-pregnant adult females and postmenarchal adolescent girls (aged 18 to 54 years) with bacterial vaginosis.
pivotal_trials.endpoint: Primary endpoint was Clinical Outcome (Clinical Responder) evaluated at the TOC/EOS visit (Day 21 to 30): normal vaginal discharge, negative 10% KOH Whiff test, and clue cells less than 20% of total epithelial cells.
pivotal_trials.n: 189 patients enrolled; primary analysis mITT population N=164 (SYM-1219 2 g N=107, placebo N=57).
pivotal_trials.result: Clinical Responder rate at Day 21-30 was 53.3% with SOLOSEC vs 19.3% with placebo (difference 34.0; 95% CI 18.7, 49.3; p<0.001). Therapeutic Responder rate was 34.6% vs 3.5% (p<0.001).

nct_ctgov.title: A Phase 3 Study of SYM-1219 Treatment of Women and Post-Menarchal Adolescent Girls With Bacterial Vaginosis

key_safety: Most common adverse reactions (incidence >=2%) were vulvo-vaginal candidiasis, headache, nausea, dysgeusia, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and vulvovaginal pruritus. In placebo-controlled trials, vulvo-vaginal candidiasis occurred in 9.6% (SOLOSEC N=197) vs 2.9% (placebo N=136); headache 3.6% vs 1.5%; nausea 3.6% vs 0.7%. No deaths occurred.
target_moa: Secnidazole is a 5-nitroimidazole antimicrobial; it enters the bacterial cell as an inactive prodrug where the nitro group is reduced by bacterial enzymes to radical anions that interfere with bacterial DNA synthesis of susceptible isolates.

advisory_committee.vote: The application was not referred to an FDA advisory committee because there were no issues that would benefit from advisory committee discussion.

summary.text: SYM-1219 (secnidazole), a 5-nitroimidazole new chemical entity, received QIDP designation (granted November 18, 2014) and Fast Track designation (granted August 12, 2015), and was reviewed under Priority review; it was approved first cycle for treatment of bacterial vaginosis in adult women, without accelerated approval.
